title: How to Lower Your Internet Bill Without Slowing Down
description: How to lower your internet bill: check the speed you need, call your provider with a simple script, drop extra fees and look for low-cost plans.
keywords: lower internet bill how to negotiate internet bill cheaper internet plans internet bill too high equipment rental fee
takeaways: Most households pay for more speed than they use. Check what you actually need first.
Call your provider, ask about current offers, and be ready to switch.
Return rented equipment and drop extras you do not use.
body:
Your internet bill rarely jumps all at once. It creeps. A promotion ends, a fee gets added, a faster tier gets sold to you during a support call, and a year later you are paying far more than the price you signed up for.

The fix is not complicated, and it does not mean putting up with slow, buffering internet. Most households can cut the bill four ways: drop charges they never meant to pay, stop renting equipment, move to the speed tier they actually use, and make one phone call with the right words ready. If money is tight, there is help available too, though one big program you may have read about is gone. This guide points you to the ones that still exist.

## Start by reading your bill properly

Pull up your latest bill, not the summary email, the full itemized one. You are looking for five things:

- The base price of your plan, and whether it says "promotional" anywhere. Promotions usually run 12 or 24 months, then the price rises on its own.
- An equipment or gateway rental fee.
- Add-ons you do not remember choosing: security software, premium tech support, device insurance, streaming bundles.
- One-off charges that repeat, like "network enhancement" or service visit fees from months ago.
- The speed on the bill, in Mbps. Write it down; you need it for the next step.

If a charge makes no sense, that is normal. Plenty of people pay for extras added during a phone call they barely remember. [The 20-minute monthly money review](/blog/monthly-money-review/) walks through this same kind of check for your whole budget, and it is worth doing once or twice a year.

## Check the speed you use, not the speed you bought

Internet plans are sold in speed tiers, and the advertising pushes you toward the top one. Gigabit this, fastest ever that. What matters is what your home actually does at the busiest moment of the day, and for most homes that is a lot less.

Try this quick audit. Run a free speed test (your provider's app has one, or search "speed test" and use the first result) at your busiest time, usually the evening, with the usual devices connected. Then think about what is happening at once in your home, and compare it with this rough guide:

| Who is online             | What is usually happening at the same time                    | Speed that usually covers it |
|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| One person, small flat        | Browsing, email, video calls, one HD stream                       | 50 to 100 Mbps                   |
| Two or three people           | Two streams, a work call, phones and laptops on top               | 100 to 300 Mbps                  |
| Four or more people           | Several streams including 4K, game downloads, multiple work calls | 300 to 500 Mbps                  |
| Very large or heavy-use homes | Constant large uploads, many 4K streams at once                   | 500 Mbps and up                  |

This is a guide, not a rule. Upload speed matters too if you are on video calls all day or post a lot of video. But if you pay for 1,000 Mbps and your household looks like row two, dropping one or two tiers will usually save money every month, and you are unlikely to feel the difference. Providers count on you never checking.

## Make the call: a script that works

Negotiating sounds awkward, but this is a routine call for providers. They have a team, often called retention or loyalty, whose whole job is offering discounts to people who might leave. You just have to reach them and ask clearly.

Before you call, have three things in front of you: your current bill, the price of the best competing offer at your address, and your account number. Then ask for the cancellations or retention department; the first person you speak to may not be able to offer much.

Here is the opening, word for word:

"Hi, I have been a customer for [number] years. My promotion ended and my bill has gone up to $[amount] a month, which is more than I can keep paying. [Competitor name] is offering [speed] Mbps for $[price] at my address. I would rather stay with you. What can you do to bring my bill down?"

If the offer is small, say this:

"Thanks, that helps a bit, but it is still more than [competitor] charges. Is there a current promotion you can put me on instead, or a plan at a lower price that keeps the speed I use?"

If they say nothing is available, finish with this:

"I understand. Before I switch, could you check once more with the retention team? If there is really nothing, I will need to set a cancellation date for [date]."

A few habits make the call go better. Stay polite the whole time; the person on the phone did not set your price. Write down the agent's name, the new price, how long it lasts, and any confirmation number. Ask when the discount expires and put that date in your calendar, because the price will rise again when it ends. If the call fails, you have lost twenty minutes, nothing more. Plenty of people repeat this call once a year.

This same approach, polite, prepared, with a real alternative in hand, works on plenty of other bills too. [How to lower your electric bill](/blog/lower-your-electric-bill/) uses a similar routine for energy costs.

## Stop paying rent on a box

Look again at that equipment fee. Renting a modem or gateway feels harmless because it is one small line on the bill, but it never stops. As an illustration, a $14 monthly rental is $168 a year, every year, for a box that often costs less than that to buy once.

Most providers let you use your own modem and router if the model is on their approved list, published on their website. Check the list before buying. When you return the rented box, get proof of the return and keep it; providers occasionally keep billing for equipment they already have back, and the receipt is how you get that fixed.

One caution: if you often need tech support and are not comfortable setting up your own kit, renting buys you a free replacement when something breaks. For everyone else, buying usually pays for itself within the first year.

## Trim the extras and take the boring discounts

While you have the bill open, cancel anything you do not use: the security suite you never installed, the streaming service bundled in that you also pay for separately, the premium support plan. Together, small charges like these can add up to the price of a whole cheaper plan. [How to cancel subscriptions you don't use](/blog/cancel-subscriptions/) covers the same habit for apps and streaming.

Also check two dull but real discounts. Many providers knock a few dollars off for autopay and paperless billing, and some offer student, senior, or veteran discounts that nobody mentions unless you ask. None of this is exciting. It is also free money for five minutes of clicking.

## If money is tight, here is the help that actually exists

### The Affordable Connectivity Program is over

A lot of older articles, and some current ones, will tell you to apply for the Affordable Connectivity Program, or ACP. Do not waste your time. According to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the ACP ended on June 1, 2024, after its funding ran out and Congress did not replace it. It had given eligible households up to $30 a month off internet service, and about 23 million households were enrolled, so its end pushed a lot of bills up at once. Anyone who offers to enroll you in the ACP today, especially for a fee, is not telling the truth. The help below is what is actually open.

### Lifeline: a federal discount that is still running

Lifeline is an older federal program, run by the Universal Service Administrative Company (USAC) for the FCC, and it is still active. It takes up to $9.25 a month off a phone or internet bill, and up to $34.25 a month for households on qualifying Tribal lands.

You qualify if someone in your household takes part in a program such as SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, Federal Public Housing Assistance, or a Veterans Pension, or if your household income is at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines. Applying is free through the National Verifier at lifelinesupport.org. One household can have one Lifeline benefit, and it goes on either your phone or your internet, not both.

### Low-cost plans run by the providers themselves

Most big providers quietly run a low-cost plan for qualifying households. One example: Xfinity's Internet Essentials costs $14.95 a month for speeds up to 75 Mbps, with a Plus version at $29.95 a month for up to 100 Mbps, equipment included, no credit check and no contract (prices checked in October 2026). AT&T, Spectrum, Cox, and others run similar plans under different names. They are rarely advertised on the home page, so search the provider's site for "low income" or ask on the phone. The FCC's own advice after the ACP ended was exactly this: call your internet company and ask whether it has a lower cost plan or a low-income program.

### State and local help

Some states add their own support on top. California, for instance, runs a LifeLine home broadband pilot that gives eligible households a credit toward broadband with participating providers. Your state public utility commission website is the place to check what exists where you live.

## What this looks like in real numbers

The figures below are an illustration with made-up numbers. Your prices will differ.

Say your bill is $90 a month: $75 for a 500 Mbps plan after its promotion ended, plus $15 to rent the gateway. You run the speed audit and find your home of three never needs more than the 200 Mbps tier, which costs $55. You buy your own gateway, so the $15 rental disappears. On the call, you get a $10 monthly discount for 12 months. Your new bill is $45 a month: $45 saved each month, $540 over a year, for one evening of effort.

| Change                                      | Monthly saving         |
|-------------------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Dropping to the speed tier you actually use     | $20                       |
| Returning the rented gateway and using your own | $15                       |
| Discount agreed on the retention call           | $10                       |
| Total                                           | $45 a month, $540 a year |

Money freed up like this is easier to use well if it has a job waiting for it. [How to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) shows how to fit a lower bill into a tight monthly budget.

## When switching beats negotiating

Sometimes the call goes nowhere: there is no competing provider on your street, or your current provider knows it. If a rival does serve your address, switching is often where the biggest savings sit, because new-customer prices are usually the lowest a company offers. Before you move, check three things: whether you are in a contract and what leaving early costs, whether the new price is a promotion and when it ends, and whether the new provider charges for installation or equipment. Compare the full first-year cost, not the headline monthly price.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I really negotiate my internet bill?

Yes. Providers expect it, and they keep staff and promotions for exactly this. You will not always get a discount, but asking costs nothing, and a competitor's price in hand makes a real difference.

### Will dropping to a slower tier make my internet feel slow?

Only if your household actually uses the speed you are giving up. If your busiest evening involves two streams and a video call, a mid-range tier handles that comfortably. Run the audit above first, and remember you can usually move back up in minutes if you judge it wrong.

### Is the Affordable Connectivity Program coming back?

Not at the moment. The FCC says the program ended on June 1, 2024 because the funding ran out, and it would take new funding from Congress to restart it. Until the FCC announces otherwise, treat any site offering ACP enrollment as out of date or worse.

### Can I get Lifeline and a low-cost provider plan at the same time?

In many cases, yes. Lifeline is a discount applied to a bill, and a provider's own low-cost plan is a separate offer, so the two can work together if the provider allows it. Ask the provider to confirm before you sign up, and remember Lifeline covers one service per household.

### How often should I repeat all this?

Once a year is plenty for most people, plus a quick check whenever your bill changes. Prices rise mainly when promotions end, so the date your discount expires is the date to act.

**Disclaimer:** This article is general information about lowering a household bill, not personal financial advice. Prices, plans, and assistance programs change and vary by address, so confirm details with your provider and on the official program websites before deciding.
